explanations.explanation: Joab son of Zeruiah marches out with David's servants and meets Abner's side by the pool of Gibeon. Keep that name handy, friend, because Joab is right in the middle of this whole story. His two brothers are on the field too. I think his day is about to get complicated.

Benaiah son of Jehoiada shows up later in David's story, as the man over the Cherethites and Pelethites (2 Samuel 8:18). Good name to know, but he isn't the one at this pool. The text says Joab son of Zeruiah marches out with David's servants. Wrong spot on the field, same army.

Uriah the Hittite is listed among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39), so I see why he came to mind. He isn't the one the text puts at Gibeon, though. Joab son of Zeruiah is the one who marches out and meets Abner's side by the pool. Nobody brings up Uriah in this passage at all.

explanations.answer: Let the young men compete before them
explanations.explanation: Abner says to Joab, “Let us have the young men get up and compete before us.” That's the whole suggestion. Notice it comes from Abner, not from Joab. The text doesn't say why he asks, so I won't guess, but I do think a contest that starts with the words 'compete' sounds friendlier than what comes next.

explanations.answer: Let the two kings meet and talk
explanations.explanation: No kings come to the pool in this scene. Abner speaks to Joab, and what he asks for is that the young men get up and compete before them. The two kings are David and Ish-bosheth, and neither one is standing by the water. A sit-down would have been a very different afternoon.

explanations.answer: Let both sides go home in peace
explanations.explanation: Going home in peace would have been a short story, friend, and the text keeps going. Abner's words to Joab are, “Let us have the young men get up and compete before us.” Nobody packs up at this point. Both sides stay right where they are, on opposite sides of the pool.

Joab doesn't turn it down at all. Right after Abner's idea, Joab replies, “Let them get up.” Quick answer, no counteroffer, no 'let me think about it.' Some people take a week to pick a restaurant, and Joab took one sentence.
Right, he agrees. Joab replies, “Let them get up.” No pushback and no haggling, just yes. Then the young men get up and are counted off.

Twelve it is. The young men are counted off, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve for David. That's an even match, twelve against twelve. Whoever counted them off made sure both sides had the same number.

Seven is a popular number in the Bible, so I get the pull. But the text counts twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve for David. Both sides get the same number, just not that one. Stick with what the verse says.

Forty would be a big crowd for a contest at a pool, friend. The text says they were counted off, twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve for David. That's twelve a side. A lot fewer than forty.

Not quite. Each man grabs his opponent and thrusts his sword into his opponent's side, and then “they all fell together.” When everyone falls together, there's no side left standing to call the winner. The text moves on and the real fighting follows.

Right, nobody wins this one. Each man grabs his opponent by the head and thrusts his sword into his opponent's side, and “they all fell together.” That leaves no clear winner. I think this is a heavy moment, and the text doesn't dress it up. The place gets a name, Helkath-hazzurim, and the battle that follows is the intense part.

explanations.answer: Abner and the men of Israel
explanations.explanation: Abner and the men of Israel are defeated by the servants of David. The text says the battle that day was intense, so this wasn't a gentle loss. The contest at the pool settled nothing, but the fighting that followed did settle this. Abner's side took the hit.

explanations.answer: Joab and the servants of David
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around, friend. The text says Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by the servants of David. Joab is on the winning side of the battle. The battle was still intense, though.

explanations.answer: The Philistines who join the fight
explanations.explanation: No Philistines show up in this passage. This fight is between the men of Abner and Ish-bosheth and the servants of David. The text says Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by the servants of David. Nobody else gets pulled into the story at Gibeon.

Asahel chases Abner, and the text says he never turns to the right or to the left while he does it. He is one of the three sons of Zeruiah, and the text calls him fleet of foot like a wild gazelle. Out of everyone on that field, he picks the commander on the other side. That's a big target for a fast runner.

Ish-bosheth, Saul's son and the king over Israel's side, isn't on the battlefield in this passage. The text sends Abner and Ish-bosheth's servants out to Gibeon, and Asahel runs after Abner. So the chase is aimed at Abner. The king stays out of the scene.

Amasa is a name from later in David's story, when Absalom makes him commander of the army (2 Samuel 17:25). He isn't anywhere in this chase. Asahel runs after Abner. Good guess for a name that sounds like it belongs in a war story.
True. Asahel chases Abner “not turning to the right or to the left in his pursuit.” He locks onto one target and keeps going. That one detail matters a lot in the verses ahead.
The text says the opposite. Asahel chased Abner “not turning to the right or to the left in his pursuit.” He's locked in the whole way. Keep an eye on that, because Abner asks him to turn.

explanations.answer: Grab one of the young men and take his gear
explanations.explanation: Abner tells him, “Turn to your right or to your left, seize one of the young men, and take his equipment for yourself.” That's the offer: pick somebody else and walk away with his gear. Abner is giving Asahel a way out. The text doesn't say why, so I won't guess.

explanations.answer: Go back and wait with his brother Joab
explanations.explanation: Abner never tells him to go back to Joab. What Abner says is, “Turn to your right or to your left, seize one of the young men, and take his equipment for yourself.” So he's pointing Asahel at a different target. Joab does come up soon, but only in Abner's next warning (2 Samuel 2:22).

explanations.answer: Drop his weapons and head home to Hebron
explanations.explanation: Nobody mentions home or dropping weapons here. Abner says, “Turn to your right or to your left, seize one of the young men, and take his equipment for yourself.” That's a different target, not a retreat. Hebron isn't named anywhere in this chase.
He doesn't take it. The text says Asahel “would not stop chasing him.” Abner gave him a way out and he stayed locked on. Abner has to warn him a second time.
Right, Asahel keeps going. The text says he “would not stop chasing him.” That's why Abner has to speak up a second time. Same runner, same target.

Abner asks, “How could I show my face to your brother Joab?” So Joab is Asahel's brother, and Abner brings him up in the warning itself. The text doesn't say what Abner is thinking beyond those words. I think he's trying hard to talk Asahel out of this.

Michal was Saul's daughter and David's wife (1 Samuel 18:27), but she isn't in this scene. Abner's question names Asahel's brother Joab. He asks, “How could I show my face to your brother Joab?” The name he brings up is family to Asahel.

David, the king the men of Judah anointed (2 Samuel 2:4), isn't the one Abner names. He asks, “How could I show my face to your brother Joab?” It's about Asahel's brother, not the king. David stays out of this chase.

The text says “every man paused when he came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died.” Everybody who reached that place stopped. The text doesn't say what any of them were thinking, but I think this is a heavy moment, and a pause fits it.

The text doesn't mention any torn robes. It says “every man paused when he came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died.” They stop at that spot. This is a quiet, heavy moment, so I'll stick with what's written.

No stones in this passage, friend. The text says “every man paused when he came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died.” They pause, and that's all it tells us. Asahel is buried later, in his father's tomb in Bethlehem.

explanations.answer: Rally to Abner and take a stand on a hill
explanations.explanation: The Benjamites rally to Abner, form a single unit, and take their stand atop a hill. They'd been on the run, and now they turn around together. Abner's side pulls itself back into one group. That's when Abner calls out to Joab.

explanations.answer: Scatter and run off in every direction
explanations.explanation: They do the opposite. The text says the Benjamites rallied to Abner, formed a single unit, and took their stand atop a hill. That's one group, not a hundred directions. They hold together.

explanations.answer: Hand Abner over to Joab and Abishai
explanations.explanation: Nobody hands anybody over. The Benjamites rally to Abner and take their stand atop a hill. They stand with him, not against him. Abner is still the one doing the talking.

explanations.answer: Tell the troops to stop chasing their brothers
explanations.explanation: Abner calls out, “How long before you tell the troops to stop pursuing their brothers?” That's his request: call off the chase. He also asks, “Must the sword devour forever?” The word 'brothers' is his, and I think it says a lot.

explanations.answer: Meet him alone on top of the hill
explanations.explanation: Abner doesn't ask Joab to climb up and meet him alone. He asks, “How long before you tell the troops to stop pursuing their brothers?” It's about the troops, not a private meeting. He's speaking to Joab from where his men are standing.

explanations.answer: Bring King David out to talk with him
explanations.explanation: David isn't part of this conversation. Abner asks Joab, “How long before you tell the troops to stop pursuing their brothers?” The request is for Joab to call off his troops. No talks with the king are mentioned.

explanations.answer: The troops would have kept chasing until morning
explanations.explanation: Joab says, “As surely as God lives,” and then, “…if you had not spoken up, the troops would have continued pursuing their brothers until morning.” So he says Abner's plea made the difference. The chase would have gone all night. After that, Joab blows the ram's horn.

explanations.answer: The troops would have stopped at sunset anyway
explanations.explanation: Joab says the opposite. His words are, “…if you had not spoken up, the troops would have continued pursuing their brothers until morning.” So Abner speaking up is what changes things. Sunset had already come, and the chase hadn't stopped.

explanations.answer: The troops would have surrounded the hill
explanations.explanation: Surrounding the hill isn't what Joab says. He says, “…if you had not spoken up, the troops would have continued pursuing their brothers until morning.” It's about how long the chase would have lasted. The text doesn't give a plan for the hill.

That's the reverse of what happens. Joab blows the ram's horn, and “all the troops stopped; they no longer pursued Israel or continued to fight.” The horn is the signal to end it. Nobody charges up the hill.
Right. Joab blows the ram's horn, and all the troops stop. The text says they “no longer pursued Israel or continued to fight.” One horn blast and the fighting is over.

Abner and his men march all night through the Arabah, cross the Jordan, march all morning, and arrive at Mahanaim. That's the same place they marched out from at the start (2 Samuel 2:12). They come back where they began. That's a long, tiring way to end up in the same spot.

Ramah isn't named anywhere in this march. The text says Abner and his men marched all night through the Arabah, crossed the Jordan, marched all morning, and arrived at Mahanaim. That's where they started from. Mahanaim is the answer.

Jericho isn't on this route in the text. Abner and his men cross the Jordan and march all morning, and they arrive at Mahanaim. That's the place they marched out from at the start. They end up right where they began.

True, and the gap is big. David's side is missing Asahel and nineteen others, but they struck down 360 Benjamites who were with Abner. That's a huge difference in numbers. It matches what the text said earlier, that Abner and the men of Israel were defeated.

The numbers say otherwise, friend. Nineteen of David's servants are missing besides Asahel, but David's men struck down 360 Benjamites who were with Abner. That's far more on Abner's side. It's a heavy count for both sides.

They bury Asahel in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. Asahel goes home to his own family, with his father. After the burial, Joab and his men march all night. The text tells us this and nothing more about it.

Hebron is where Joab and his men go after the burial. They reach it at daybreak, after marching all night. But Asahel is buried in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. Two places, both in this verse, easy to swap.

Gibeon is where the fighting started, by the pool. Asahel is buried somewhere else. The text says David's men took him and buried him in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. He goes home, not back to the battlefield.
True. The text says the war between the house of Saul and the house of David “was protracted.” That means it dragged on. Gibeon didn't end it, and the story keeps going.
The text says otherwise. The war between the house of Saul and the house of David “was protracted.” That's a long, drawn-out war. Joab's horn ended that day's chase, but not the war.

explanations.answer: David grows stronger and Saul's house grows weaker
explanations.explanation: The text says David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker. The two sides are moving in opposite directions. The war drags on, but it isn't an even race. And the sons born to David in Hebron come right after that line.

explanations.answer: Saul's house grows stronger and David grows weaker
explanations.explanation: That's flipped, friend. The text says David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker. Saul's house is the one slipping. David is the one climbing.

explanations.answer: Both sides keep growing weaker and weaker
explanations.explanation: Only one side is shrinking. The text says David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker. Two sides, two different directions. David's side is the one getting stronger.
